trigger.insight: The inbound said portal, but the real trigger was a new CFO whose first close took nine days because two people were matching deposits by hand. The rep's own portal story doesn't hold together: first they were 'building a portal', later it is 'off the shelf with a plugin'. The checkout opportunity was never the buying reason. It was the IT-side reason that happened to reach us first.
trigger.messaging: For finance-led buyers, open on close time and manual deposit matching (lead with M9) instead of checkout, even when the inbound mentions a portal.

decider.insight: Ines decided, and two things back that up: the IT director's own words and her signature. The first proposal was written for the recommender (checkout, APIs), so it died on the decider's first page and the deal stalled for three weeks. Our default proposal is built for the technical buyer, and here that buyer had no budget authority.
decider.messaging: Make page one of every proposal a finance-owner summary (days to close, unmatched deposits, hours spent matching), with APIs and checkout pushed to an appendix.

competitor.insight: The only thing we know the incumbent said is a rate offer, and the CFO rejected it as an answer to a question she hadn't asked. That makes price the wrong battlefield against a bank-bundled incumbent here. The rep said 'not much' changed after the bank call, yet a new question appeared: a named contact, because her bank rep had changed and she didn't know who the new one was. That is the incumbent's real weakness, and our support message (tiered response times) doesn't speak to it.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-bundled incumbents, don't lead with rates; position on 'you'll always know who your person is' and reframe M5 around a named contact, not response-time tiers.

message.insight: M1 (global, every currency) and M2 (built for developers) landed in silence with a customer that sells to restaurants in three states and has a four-person IT team that isn't building anything. Only M9 got a reaction, and it was strong enough that the CFO interrupted the demo and asked to see it with their own data. Our standard deck leads with the two messages that are irrelevant to this buyer and hides the one that sells.
message.messaging: Build a first-call variant for non-technical, domestic businesses that opens with M9 payout-to-ERP reconciliation and drops M1/M2 from the opening.

decided.insight: The deal turned when the value case was built from the customer's statements, hours and write-offs, so the CFO owned the number rather than discounting a vendor's claim. A generic 'independent economic impact study' (M6) is exactly the 'yours, not mine' kind of number she would have dismissed. The rep had the deal at 20 percent even after the decider said 'go back' and asked for a demo on her own data, which was the clearest buying signal in the deal. The rep can't recall the exact figure, so the win's central artifact isn't preserved.
decided.messaging: Rework M6 from citing an external study to an offer: give us one month of statements and we'll price your manual matching and unmatched-deposit write-offs.

gaps.insight: M8 ('trusted by leading businesses') failed in practice: we had no wholesale or distributor reference, and the retail story we sent was dismissed outright. She raised it twice, so we won despite the gap, not because it didn't matter. Branch counter reporting across 14 branches got only a slide, and the transcript doesn't say whether that part delivered. That makes it an unproven promise inside a deal that includes branch card processing.
gaps.messaging: Source a wholesale/distributor reference (ideally this customer, once live) and add a live demo of counter and online payouts landing in one report to M3/M9 proof.

language.insight: The buyer's vocabulary is deposits, month-end and knowing where the money is. Ours is infrastructure, payments and global growth. She describes our winning feature as an outcome (visibility, a shorter close), while we describe it as a mechanism (payouts reconcile to transactions).
language.messaging: Rewrite M9 in the buyer's words, e.g. know where every deposit is and close month-end without the archaeology, and use 'deposits' rather than 'payouts' or 'payments' with finance buyers.

gaps.question: What was the exact dollar value of the business case Wen built?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen for the model built from the customer's statements (hours, cost basis, write-offs) so it can become a reusable template and proof point.

gaps.question: What, if anything, did Fiserv or the bank show or offer beyond a rate review?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines (or Paul) in a post-sale check-in whether the bank came back with anything beyond rates and what would have kept them.

gaps.question: What changed in their questions after they talked to the bank?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana whether the named-contact request changed how she positioned support, and whether Ines raised any other new concerns after the bank call.

gaps.question: Did branch counter card readers actually land in the same report as the portal, and has branch volume moved?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen or the implementation lead whether the 14 branches are live and reconciling in the same report, since this was only shown on a slide.

gaps.question: Is the distributor reference still owed, and would this customer become one?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana whether Ines still expects the reference call and whether she would act as a distributor reference once month-end close improves.

close.rep_takeaway: When the inbound names a project (like a portal), ask early who loses sleep over the money side and whose process is broken. Here the decider was in finance, and a portal-first proposal cost weeks. Treat a decider interrupting a demo with 'go back' and asking for her own data as a strong buying signal, not a 20-percent deal. Then save the value model you build with them, because it is the win's best proof.
